title: Modern Chinese Grammar
full_title: Modern Chinese Grammar: Words, Phrases and Sentences
tagline: What grammar is, parts of speech, function words, phrases, sentence constituents, sentence patterns and types, special constructions, complex sentences, and faulty sentences
summary: Chinese has almost no inflection, so its grammar lies in word order and function words, which native speakers use effortlessly but rarely analyse. This course describes the grammar of modern Chinese: the parts of speech and the function words, how phrases are built, the constituents and patterns of sentences, special constructions such as the 把 and 被 sentences, complex sentences, and how to find and correct faulty sentences.
overview: Chinese has no case endings, no conjugations, no grammatical gender — and for that very reason a grammar of Chinese is a grammar of word order, function words and word classes that can switch jobs on the fly. This course builds the descriptive machinery of modern Mandarin grammar as taught in the university mainstream (the Huang–Liao tradition): morpheme to phrase to sentence, with distributional tests (substitution, expansion, contrast) instead of inherited Latin templates.

We take up, in order: the content words (noun, verb, adjective, numeral–classifier, pronoun, adverb) and their notorious boundary disputes; the function words (prepositions, conjunctions, the three shi particles 的地得, mood particles); phrase structures (subject–predicate, verb–object, modifier–head, verb–complement, serial-verb and the like) and immediate-constituent analysis; sentence constituents and their extraction tests; sentence types (subject-predicate vs subjectless, the four moods); special constructions (把, 被, existential and locative-inverted sentences, serial verbs, pivots, 是, comparisons); complex sentences (coordination vs subordination, the multi-functional 的 and 得 relations, clause sequences without conjunctions); and finally the diagnostic clinic of病句 correction and the writing-quality discipline of the language-normalisation tradition.

No prior grammar training is assumed; the course assumes the vocabulary lessons (word/homophone/word-boundary disputes) and treats Mandarin phonology lightly. By the end you should be able to parse any sentence two ways on purpose — and say which reading is right and why.
outcomes: apply distributional tests (substitution, expansion, minimal contrast) to decide a word's class and a string's structure
draw the word-class map of Mandarin with its hard cases (time-nouns, difference/like verbs, adjectives vs stative verbs)
analyse phrases by immediate constituents and mark the structural relations (SB, VO, AV, VN, and the like)
identify the seven sentence constituents and run the 提取法 and 加线法 on a long sentence
classify sentence types by mood and by structure, including subjectless and one-word sentences
derive the constructional meanings of 把, 被, 是, existential and locative-inverted sentences, and their formal requirements
diagnose ambiguity with structure trees and explain coordination vs subordination in complex sentences
detect and repair the twelve families of病句 with minimal-edit principles

chapters.title: What grammar is
chapters.summary: Grammatical units and relations, the characteristics of Chinese grammar, and the main systems of description since the *Mashi Wentong* of 1898.

chapters.title: Parts of speech
chapters.summary: Nouns, verbs, adjectives, numerals and classifiers, pronouns and adverbs, how they are told apart by their grammatical function, and words that belong to two classes.

chapters.title: Function words
chapters.summary: Prepositions, conjunctions, the structural particles 的, 地 and 得, the aspect particles 了, 着 and 过, and modal particles.

chapters.title: Phrases
chapters.summary: Subject–predicate, verb–object, modifier–head, verb–complement and coordinate phrases, and analysing phrases layer by layer.

chapters.title: Sentence constituents
chapters.summary: Subject, predicate, object, attributive, adverbial and complement, with the many kinds of complement that Chinese uses.

chapters.title: Sentence patterns and types
chapters.summary: Subject–predicate and subjectless sentences, and statements, questions, commands and exclamations.

chapters.title: Special constructions
chapters.summary: The 把 and 被 sentences, existential sentences, serial-verb and pivotal constructions, and comparative sentences.

chapters.title: Complex sentences
chapters.summary: Coordinate and subordinate relations between clauses, the connectives that mark them, multi-layered complex sentences, and the run-on style (流水句) of Chinese.

chapters.title: Finding and correcting faulty sentences
chapters.summary: Mismatched constituents, wrong word order, missing or redundant parts, misused connectives and ambiguity, and a method for correcting them.

history.title: Mashi Wentong
history.detail: The first systematic grammar of classical Chinese, modelled on Latin case and part-of-speech logic, proved by imitation that Chinese grammar could be described at all — and set the agenda (what counts as subject, how to classify words) that a century of native scholarship then rewrote.

history.title: A grammar of the spoken language
history.detail: Liu Shuyu's Outline of the Grammar of the National Language transferred the description from literary model to living Mandarin — the founding act of modern Chinese grammar as a school subject.

history.title: Canghai Yiwai
history.detail: A People's Daily column of corrected essays (from June 1951) tied grammatical purity to public writing and launched the normalisation campaign that still frames faulty-sentence diagnosis in schools.

history.title: Language reform conference
history.detail: The national conference on language reform set the agenda (standardise pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar; simplify script) that grammar textbooks have served ever since.

history.title: Promotion of Putonghua
history.detail: State Council directions defined Putonghua (Beijing pronunciation as norm, northern dialects as base, classic modern writings as grammatical model) — the legal-grade anchor of what counts as grammatical.

history.title: The university standard grammar
history.detail: A college textbook by Huang Borong and Liao Xudong fixed the teaching system of word classes, phrase types and the three-level grammatical scale that most Chinese classrooms still use.

history.title: New frameworks enter
history.detail: The 1980s imported structural, generative and functional syntax in waves; native-language syntax research moved from parsing essays to testing theories on Chinese facts.

history.title: The language law
history.detail: The law on spoken and written language made the standardised norm a civic obligation in public domains, closing the circle between grammar pedagogy and language policy.

references.title: 《马氏文通》
references.note: The founding text; read for its questions more than its answers.

references.title: 《国语语法》
references.note: First grammar of living Mandarin; still witty on word-class puzzles.

references.title: 《中国文法要略》
references.note: A master's balanced account of form and function; the essays behind the normalisation era.

references.title: A Grammar of Spoken Chinese
references.note: Chao's structural description of the spoken language: the model of distributional method applied with elegance.

references.title: Mandarin Chinese: A Functional Reference Grammar
references.authors: Charles N. Li & Sandra A. Thompson
references.note: The functionalist reference: information flow, topics, aspect — Chinese explained on its own terms.

references.title: 《现代汉语》(下册)
references.note: The standard university grammar; this course follows its terminology and its three-level scale.
